content:
Hi,

I was looking through mathlib’s PDE-adjacent analysis files, and it seems there is already some useful groundwork (e.g. SobolevInequality, Laplacian/harmonic-function files, LaxMilgram, and the distribution / Schwartz / tempered-distribution setup), but there is still so much missing in theoretical PDE.

In particular, I didn’t find obvious API for bounded-domain Sobolev spaces / weak derivatives, or results such as Poincaré inequality, Morrey / Sobolev-to-Hölder embeddings, or Rellich–Kondrachov. I also didn’t see much around named PDEs or calculus of variations. There is much in Evans' PDE book that has yet to be formalized. Of course, beyond this there are also specific theorems about classes of PDE, such as from Terence Tao's book on dispersive PDE that could be formalized later.

I’d be interested in contributing some things in this direction. Some ideas for small first additions:

  • some weak derivative API and general Sobolev spaces

  • basic solutions to PDEs like heat equation

  • helper lemmas interfacing with the existing Hölder infrastructure,

  • smooth-function Poincaré inequality

  • or some additional basic lemmas/constructions in the distribution theory files.

Would this be a reasonable direction, and should I open one or more issues with more specific proposed statements? Is anyone else interested in this kind of thing?

Thanks!

Note:

  • There seems to be a workshop here https://www.slmath.org/workshops/1180#overview_workshop on contributing to PDE in Mathlib but not much significant progress since then
Note that work on Sobolev spaces is understand --- both in #33329 (using Fourier analysis) and #32305 (using classical distributions).
(The latter did in fact start after the SLMath workshop, and the discussions there were helpful for the project.)

I would also like to move faster... the reality is that most people involved have other obligations also (teaching, supervision, research, admin/service work, etc. --- and reviewing in mathlib, other projects etc.).
@Moritz Doll is working on Sobolev spaces using Fourier analysis; @Filippo A. E. Nuccio, @Floris van Doorn and I are working on classical Sobolev spaces.
@Anatole Dedecker is working on classical distributions. I don't know where new contributions would be helpful, and where it's mostly a matter of cleaning up and merging existing results.
Basic PDE theory is certainly missing - if there are classical results that can be formalised already, that would be a great addition!

A general version of the Sobolev inequality, and deducing Sobolev embedding, is on my list of things (after we have Sobolev spaces). If you'd like to work in this direction, we should coordinate carefully --- or perhaps, you can pick something else from the vast selection of yet unformalised things?
Finally, let me emphasize: PDE theory is missing a lot, so I'm very happy about new people joining --- there is enough to do for everybody!

Thank you @Michael Rothgang ! This is very helpful. Sorry for my confusion as I'm new to contributing to Mathlib, but I would love to contribute in these areas as I have a good amount of free time currently. As you said I should probably avoid Sobolev spaces / weak derivatives since there's ongoing work there. Do you have any suggestions for areas in basic PDE theory that would be especially helpful to work on and where I could get started easily (without requiring Sobolev etc)?

Some ideas if any make sense to you:

  • maybe a file for the Heat equation (define Gaussian kernel, prove smoothness, prove satisfies the heat equation)
  • similar for Laplace equation, wave equation
  • poincaré inequality for some simple domains (should just require Jensen's, eventually can expand once we have Sobolev spaces and Rellich-Kondrachov etc)
    -- maybe good starting points: mean-zero poincare on a 1D interval, then on a convex bounded domain, or L^infinity poincare on convex sets

Thanks again for your help!

For the Laplace equation idea, a starting point could be to

  • define classical formulas for fundamental solution
  • prove ContDiffOn R^d \ {0}
  • prove harmonic on R^d \ {0}
    (none of this should require distributions so far, there's already work on harmonic functions)
    Then later after more support for distributions are added we can expand to prove it is the fundamental solution
One comment to avoid you frustration: writing Rd\R^dRd is not the best start if you want to contribute to Mathlib. You should probably think about a finite dimensional real inner product space.

Thanks! Just to clarify you mean that I should keep things as general as possible right? Though for the Laplace fundamental solution the explicit formula really does depend on the dimension and Euclidean space (e.g. cd∣x∣2−dc_d |x|^{2-d}cd​∣x∣2−d) so I was imagining starting in Rd\R^dRd for that

Hi @Aditya Ramabadran! Happy to see people interested in PDEs :). I have been following the current developments of distributions closely as I need them for a project. I think a good starting point to get used to the Mathlib way of things is probably to read and understand the implementation in progress for distributions. The standard is you'll need to adopt a similar level of generality for your contributions, it is a bit of getting used to. There are a few PRs to review, there might be a few simple things to do as well.

Thanks @Laura Monk that makes sense! I will read through the current implementations

I was also wondering if there's a central place to see what people are working on behind the scenes, I read this thread and it seems like a lot of people are working privately on distribution theory, Fredholm operators, and also general/heat/wave stuff for PDE:

In fact a lot happened behind the scenes recently in a private channel associated to the lean pde workshop a few weeks ago, including formalisation of a general pde, the heat and wave equations and some solutions etc.

I was also wondering if I could be added to this and observe what people are working on before starting to find small ways to start contributing :)

If you look into the distribution theory files, you can see that almost everything is phrased for abstract vector spaces, even when the dimension matters.
On the fundamental solution, I think putting work into the explicit formulas would be good, proving regularity is a bit unnecessary because that follows from abstract theory.
One other good project would be homogeneous distributions (there is a chapter in Hörmander 1) or the principal value.
There is a good reason why we don't have a lot that actually mentions PDEs explicitly yet: to do things properly you need a lot of functional analysis and there are still a lot of results missing (interpolation, Fredholm theory, Spectral theory). Formalising specific PDEs is good to see that we are on the right track, but it does not bring us closer to research level, whereas the abstract theory does.

Hi @Aditya Ramabadran I've run into a very similar issue from the downstream side.

I've been working on a Lean 4 formalization of an elliptic BVP existence argument on compact Riemannian manifolds, and in the process I ran into several pieces of PDE/functional-analytic infrastructure that aren't in Mathlib yet. For my own project, I isolated them as explicit assumptions so I could still check that the proof architecture composed correctly.

The main gaps I hit were things like:

  • Schaefer / Leray–Schauder type fixed-point machinery
  • strong maximum principles for elliptic operators
  • Schauder estimates / Hölder-space infrastructure on manifolds
  • sub/supersolution theory in ordered Banach spaces
  • Krein–Rutman / principal eigenvalue existence

So from one downstream perspective, there's definitely demand for quite a bit beyond Sobolev-space foundations. I don't mean this as a suggestion for mathlib style - just as evidence that once the analytic foundations mature, there are already fairly classical PDE arguments waiting downstream.

If useful as a reference for the kind of dependency chain that shows up downstream, the project is here: https://github.com/Project-Navi/cd-formalization - but the main point is just that these missing pieces appear quickly once you try to formalize even fairly standard elliptic existence arguments.

Hi @Aditya Ramabadran, and thanks for your interest! As Michael has said I am currently working on the very basics of (classical, not tempered) distribution theory. Things have not moved in the last few months because I keep getting distracted and have a PhD to do, but I've just restarted progress in this area last week.

Right now I don't really have anything interesting to delegate, but here are some very basic things that need to be done:

  • prove docs#ContinuousEval for docs#ContDiffMapSupportedIn, deduce docs#ContinuousEvalConst for docs#TestFunction, and use it to define the dirac distribution (in the classical sense)
  • construct the (continuous linear) map from D\mathcal{D}D to S\mathcal{S}S, as well as the linear map from S′\mathcal{S}'S′ to D′\mathcal{D}'D′ (unfortunately this won't be continuous because of different choices of topology)
Thank you @Anatole Dedecker , this is helpful! I am also working on a few things in my blueprint, related to compactly supported distributions. I will send talk about it here when I am ready to :).

Aditya Ramabadran said in #mathlib4 > PDE Theory:

Thanks! Just to clarify you mean that I should keep things as general as possible right? Though for the Laplace fundamental solution the explicit formula really does depend on the dimension and Euclidean space (e.g. cd∣x∣2−dc_d |x|^{2-d}cd​∣x∣2−d) so I was imagining starting in Rd\R^dRd for that

To answer this more explicitly, this is not only a question of generality. Even if you are only interested about Rd\R^dRd, you should work in a finite dimensional inner product space, because Mathlib is fond about type aliases so a lot of spaces that a mathematician would call Rd\R^dRd are not litterally Rd\R^dRd.

One more piece of prior work: in October, we managed to state the fundamental solution of the heat equation. Here's the 1D proof:

import Mathlib

noncomputable section

open InnerProductSpace
open scoped Real

/-- A definition of classical solutions to the 1D heat equation. -/
def IsClassical1DHeatSolution (U : Set ℝ) (u : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ContDiffOn ℝ 2 (fun xt : ℝ × ℝ ↦ u xt.1 xt.2) (U ×ˢ Set.Ioi 0)
    ∧ ∀ x ∈ U, ∀ t, 0 < t → deriv (fun s ↦ u x s) t - Laplacian.laplacian (fun y ↦ u y t) x = 0

/-! Let's check a 1D solution. -/

/-- The fundamental solution to the 1D heat equation. -/
def Ψ x t := (√(4 * π * t))⁻¹ * rexp (- x^2 / (4 * t))

/-- First derivative of Ψ with respect to time. -/
lemma deriv_Ψ_t {x t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    deriv (fun t ↦ Ψ x t) t = Ψ x t * (-2/t + x^2/t^2) / 4 := by
  simp_rw [Ψ]
  rw [deriv_fun_mul, deriv_fun_inv'', deriv_sqrt, deriv_const_mul, deriv_id'', deriv_exp,
    deriv_fun_div, deriv_const, deriv_const_mul, deriv_id'']
  · rw [Real.sq_sqrt (by positivity)]
    grind
  any_goals fun_prop (disch := positivity)
  all_goals positivity

/-- First derivative of Ψ with respect to space. -/
lemma deriv_Ψ_x {x t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    deriv (fun x ↦ Ψ x t) x = Ψ x t * (-x / (2 * t)) := by
  simp_rw [Ψ]
  simp only [deriv_const_mul_field']
  rw [mul_assoc _ _ (-x / (2 * t))]
  congr
  rw [deriv_exp (by fun_prop)]
  simp only [deriv_div_const, deriv.fun_neg', differentiableAt_fun_id, deriv_fun_pow,
    Nat.cast_ofNat, Nat.add_one_sub_one, pow_one, deriv_id'', mul_one, mul_eq_mul_left_iff,
    Real.exp_ne_zero, or_false]
  field_simp
  ring

/-- Ψ is differentiable in space. -/
@[fun_prop]
lemma differentiableAt_Ψ (x t : ℝ) : DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun x ↦ Ψ x t) x := by
  unfold Ψ
  fun_prop

/-- Second derivative of Ψ with respect to space. -/
lemma deriv2_Ψ_x {x t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    iteratedDeriv 2 (fun x ↦ Ψ x t) x = Ψ x t * (-2/t + x^2/t^2) / 4 := by
  rw [iteratedDeriv_succ, iteratedDeriv_one] -- copilot wrote that
  suffices deriv (fun x ↦ Ψ x t * (-x / (2 * t))) x = Ψ x t * (-2 / t + x ^ 2 / t ^ 2) / 4 by
    convert this using 2
    ext x
    exact deriv_Ψ_x ht
  rw [deriv_fun_mul (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop), deriv_Ψ_x ht]
  simp only [deriv_div_const, deriv_neg'']
  grind

/-- Ψ is twice continuously differentiable on ℝ × (0, ∞). -/
lemma condDiff_two_Ψ : ContDiffOn ℝ 2 (fun xt : ℝ × ℝ ↦ Ψ xt.1 xt.2) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Ioi 0) := by
  simp_rw [Ψ]
  rintro ⟨x, t⟩ ht
  simp only [Set.mem_prod, Set.mem_univ, Set.mem_Ioi, true_and] at ht
  fun_prop (disch := positivity)

/-- Ψ is a classical solution to the 1D heat equation on ℝ × (0, ∞). -/
theorem isClassical1DHeatSolution_Ψ :
    IsClassical1DHeatSolution (Set.univ : Set ℝ) Ψ := by
  constructor
  · exact condDiff_two_Ψ
  · intros x hx t ht
    rw [laplacian_eq_iteratedDeriv_real (F := ℝ), deriv_Ψ_t ht, deriv2_Ψ_x ht]
    ring
Very cool! Does this work in a more general setting?
I also wrote down the n-dimensional statement. (The proof gets hairier, and I didn't finish it.) I'm trying to find it now...

Ok, it appears harder to find the file I had. From what I remember,

  • the domain had a spatial component Fin n → ℝ,
  • the fundamental solution involves a factor of n/2 --- you'll have to experiment which of the various spellings is the least annoying (w.r.t. coercions),
  • you'll need to speak about more general derivatives.

Regarding "what's happening informally": my experience is that many things are mentioned on zulip (but zulip is vast), and sometimes hints of projects are scarce. Asking in a thread (like you did!) is the best strategy right now.

A key question I've been postponing is: how do we transition to manifolds? For example, is the plan to eventually replace docs#TestFunction by the manifold version, or should that be a different type?

Hi @Aditya Ramabadran , very nice to see interest in this area. I don't have much to add to what my colleagues have already said, but let me stress that the above suggestion by @Michael Rothgang is really crucial: the more you discuss your work, and your struggles, on Zulip, the better you'll advance and you'll receive help.

I've moved all the messages to a dedicated channel (see above): we were (interestingly) discussing about the impact of AI, perhaps even on analysis, but the topic was no longer about PDE's.

Just a note from the classical side -- I have formalised three 1D PDE results (weak solutions of conservation laws, Burgers gradient blow-up, KdV soliton) using only elementary calculus, Fubini, and ODEs over Mathlib, with zero sorry. Might complement the concrete-PDE direction discussed here.

Repo: github.com/Alektronnik/M4TH -- packages ConservationLaws, BurgersBlowUp, KdV.

(I also posted a standalone topic with more detail in #mathlib4.)
